reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) supports thermal-aging-induced phase separation and interstitial-driven segregation/softening in a specific RHEA at 700°C, but it does not address the key mechanistic premises that mechanical loading (stress) drives this segregation, that the resulting precipitates are brittle intermetallics, or that this leads to brittle fracture and toughness loss. The hypothesis extends the evidence into unsupported claims about stress-assisted kinetics and fracture mechanisms.
premises: Single-phase RHEAs can phase-separate and form precipitates at intermediate temperatures (700–800°C).
Trace interstitial impurities (O, N) promote phase segregation during thermal aging.
Interstitial-driven segregation depletes the matrix, causing softening.
Stress-assisted diffusion can localize solute segregation at grain boundaries and dislocations.
Brittle intermetallic precipitates at boundaries cause loss of toughness and brittle fracture.
